items.stem: Your users are in Metro Manila and your servers are in Virginia, 13,700 km away. Light in fiber travels about 200,000 km per second. What is the shortest possible round-trip time on a perfect network?

options.text: About 137 ms.
options.feedback: The round trip covers 2 × 13,700 km = 27,400 km. Dividing by 200,000 km per second gives 0.137 seconds.

options.text: About 69 ms.
options.feedback: This is the one-way time. A response needs the request to travel there and the reply to travel back.

options.text: About 1,370 ms.
options.feedback: This is ten times too large. 27,400 km divided by 200,000 km per second is 0.137 seconds.

options.text: About 0 ms, because the server is fast.
options.feedback: Server speed does not change how long the signal takes to travel. Distance sets a minimum that no code can go below.

items.stem: Before you try it: a page needs five round trips and your handler takes 40 ms. With servers in Singapore the time to first byte is about 230 ms. What will it be with servers in Virginia?

options.text: About 1,080 ms.
options.feedback: Each round trip grows from about 38 ms to about 208 ms. Five round trips plus 40 ms for the handler gives about 1,078 ms.

options.text: About 270 ms.
options.feedback: This treats distance as a small extra cost. Every one of the five round trips gets longer.

options.text: About 230 ms, because the handler time is the same.
options.feedback: The handler is the same, but distance applies to every round trip.

options.text: About 140 ms, because the minimum round trip is only 137 ms.
options.feedback: The minimum applies to one round trip on a perfect network. A real network takes about 1.5 times that, and a page needs five round trips.

items.try: Move the Region slider from Singapore to Virginia (US East) and read the time to first byte.

items.stem: Your app runs on three machines behind a load balancer, all in one data center. The data center loses power. What happens?

options.text: The site goes down, because all three machines were in the same building.
options.feedback: A load balancer sends traffic away from a failed machine. When the whole building fails, there is no healthy machine to send traffic to.

options.text: The load balancer moves traffic to the two remaining machines.
options.feedback: All three machines lost power together, so none remain.

options.text: The site stays up, because a load balancer protects against every kind of failure.
options.feedback: A load balancer protects against a machine failing. It cannot move work to a building that is also down.

options.text: The site slows down but keeps serving users from the backup copy.
options.feedback: There is no backup copy in this setup. Everything is in one data center.

items.stem: Your app uses the multi-region option with a standby in Tokyo, and the primary region fails. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The site returns after 10 to 30 minutes, and up to 30 seconds of writes may be lost.
options.feedback: Tokyo is 3,000 km away, so its copy is updated after each write is confirmed. A failure can lose the newest writes, and switching over takes time.

options.text: The site never goes down, and no data is lost because Tokyo has a full copy.
options.feedback: Switching to the standby takes minutes. Asynchronous copying also means the newest writes may not have reached Tokyo.

options.text: The site returns in under a minute with no data lost, as in the multi-AZ option.
options.feedback: These figures belong to the multi-AZ option, where the two buildings are milliseconds apart.

options.text: The site is down until the primary region is repaired, however long that takes.
options.feedback: The standby in Tokyo exists so that the site can run while the primary region is down.

items.stem: Every user of your capstone is in Metro Manila, and your budget is small. Which setup does this panel recommend?

options.text: A Singapore region, using multi-AZ if the provider offers it by default.
options.feedback: Singapore gives a comfortable time to first byte, and multi-AZ protects against a data center failure at little extra cost.

options.text: Multi-region with a standby in Tokyo, to be safe.
options.feedback: Multi-region doubles the cost, needs code for conflicting writes and accepts a data-loss window. It suits cases where a region outage costs more than running two of everything.

options.text: Virginia, because it is the most widely used region.
options.feedback: Virginia is 13,700 km from your users and gives more than a second to first byte.

options.text: One machine in one data center, with a nightly backup.
options.feedback: This is the cheapest option, but a single data center failure takes the site down for hours.
